objectives: Distinguish linear selectivity in simple cells from phase invariance in complex cells, and explain why an even-symmetric response can drive the first-order STA toward zero.
Derive phase invariance step by step from the two linear outputs of a quadrature pair while stating the amplitude and orientation dependence that remains.
Separate task training of an optimized model from evaluation of neural predictivity, and design a comparison that never leaks test neural data.
Write the fixed-point equations and nullclines of an E/I rate network and analyze how surround input can produce suppression without raising inhibitory rate.

prerequisiteBridge: Imagine a Gabor-like filter as a template of alternating positive and negative bands. The inner product is positive when bright bars align with positive weights and dark bars with negative weights. Translating the grating by half a period reverses the sign. A simple cell may retain this phase sign, while a complex cell often fires at several phases of the same orientation. If the response is identical for s and -s, positive and negative examples occur in pairs among spike-triggered stimuli and cancel in an ordinary average. The neuron remains selective; the first-order statistic uses the wrong coordinates.

Comparing a model with neural data involves two distinct fits. First, network weights may be trained on a task such as object classification, defining representation \(z(x)\). Second, part of the neural dataset fits a simple mapping from z to neuronal responses, which is evaluated on stimuli excluded from that fit. Classification accuracy asks whether the network performs the task. Neural predictivity asks whether an internal representation relates to recorded responses through a linear or otherwise specified mapping. The scores may correlate, but neither logically guarantees the other.

E/I dynamics require only first-order differential equations and intersections of two lines. Treat \(r_{E}\) and \(r_{I}\) as time-varying population firing rates. Points satisfying \(dr/dt=0\) form a nullcline; the two nullclines intersect at a fixed point. Arrow direction follows the signs of the derivatives. Stability means that the vector field pushes small perturbations back, not that one drawn curve looks steep. Eigenvalues of the linearization provide the local criterion.

modules.title: From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy
paragraphs: This section links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection.

The challenge for a complex cell is phase invariance. If it responds strongly to both positive and negative phases of a grating at one orientation, a linear STA averages the two spike-triggered groups toward zero. This section instead uses two filters separated by 90° of spatial phase—a quadrature pair. As input phase changes, their linear outputs carry energy in turn like two coordinates. Squaring and adding reads vector radius rather than angle.

For a grating matching orientation and spatial frequency, let the two filter projections be \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), where A depends on contrast and match quality and \(\phi\) is stimulus phase. Energy \(E=L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}=A^{2}\) is independent of \(\phi\). The invariance is conditional: changing orientation or frequency lowers the common projection amplitude A, and changing contrast changes A and hence E. The energy model removes phase, not all stimulus information.

STC can identify these two feature axes as abnormal directions of spike-triggered covariance because spikes select a large radius in the two-dimensional subspace rather than one signed mean direction. The model is still a descriptive cascade of two linear filters, squaring nonlinearities, summation, and perhaps an output nonlinearity. Reproducing several complex-cell responses does not prove that biological synapses implement four anatomically separate stages.
keyPoints: Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity.
A complex-cell energy model uses the squared sum of a quadrature pair to turn stimulus phase into an ignored two-dimensional angle.
A zero STA can coexist with strong selectivity; examine covariance or a multifilter subspace in that case.

derivation.title: Why Quadrature Energy Is Invariant to Phase
derivation.setup: For a grating of fixed orientation and frequency, let two normalized filters separated by 90° of phase produce \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\).

steps.title: Write the Sum of Squares
steps.explanation: The energy stage squares each signed projection separately and adds the two nonnegative results.

steps.title: Factor Out the Common Amplitude
steps.explanation: A does not depend on the current phase, so it can be factored outside the parentheses, leaving the unit-circle identity.

steps.title: Apply the Unit-Circle Identity
steps.explanation: cos\(\phi\) and sin\(\phi\) are the two coordinates of a unit vector. Their squared sum is 1, leaving energy \(A^{2}\).

symbolNotes: A still changes with contrast, orientation mismatch, frequency mismatch, and receptive-field overlap.
Exact invariance assumes truly quadrature filters with matched gains; biological measurements generally approximate this condition.
derivation.unitsCheck: If linear outputs use drive units of spikes/s, their squared sum has \(drive^{2}\) units. A final output nonlinearity can map it back to firing rate.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(A=0\), every phase gives \(E=0\). If the second filter has twice the gain of the first, the squared sum varies with \(\phi\) and phase invariance fails.

workedExample.title: Equal Energy at Three Phases
workedExample.problem: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\).
workedExample.result: The linear outputs differ at all three phases, but energy equals 16 each time.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Every pair (L1,L2) lies on a circle of radius 4, and the sum of squares is the squared radius.

pitfalls: Concluding from a near-zero complex-cell STA that the stimulus does not drive the cell, while ignoring positive-negative cancellation under an even nonlinearity.
Calling square-and-sum invariant to every transformation; it is only approximately invariant to phase rotations within the covered subspace.

modules.title: Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests
paragraphs: The logic spans two data domains. A network first learns weights from a task dataset and classification loss; its feature hierarchy reflects both task and architecture. Freeze the network, compute layer features \(z(x)\) for experimental stimuli, and fit a constrained mapping from z to response r using training neural trials—for example, a ridge-regularized linear readout. Report predictive correlation or explained variance only on held-out stimuli or trials.

High task accuracy does not define neural similarity. Many internal coordinate systems can implement the same classification boundary; networks that rely on texture or shape may score similarly on labels. Predictivity also depends on mapping flexibility. A nonlinear mapper with far more parameters than observations can fit almost any representation to training responses. Use simple mappings of equal complexity and identical cross-validation for every candidate layer.

Let feature matrix \(Z\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\) contain one stimulus per row and one model feature per column, and neural matrix \(R\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}\) contain one neuron per column. Fit \(B\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\) by minimizing \(||ZB-R||^{2}\). B aligns coordinate systems but does not change the task representation of the original network. Compare models with the same N, neurons, noise ceiling, and regularization-selection rule.

Neural data contain trial noise, so single-trial correlation cannot reach 1 even when a model captures all reproducible stimulus-driven signal. A noise ceiling estimated from split-half reliability approximates the predictable limit. Report uncertainty with raw and ceiling-normalized predictivity. If one layer scores higher, the justified claim is limited to the current stimuli, area, mapping family, and measurement noise—not mechanistic equivalence to the whole visual system.
keyPoints: Task training determines the representation; a neural readout and held-out evaluation test its alignment with biological responses.
Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately.
Mapping complexity, data splits, and the noise ceiling materially affect the comparison.

derivation.title: Deriving a Neural Readout from a Least-Squares Objective
derivation.setup: For a simple derivation without regularization, choose B to minimize \(L(B)=||ZB-R||_F^{2}\) for model features Z and neural responses R.

steps.title: Write the Matrix Gradient
steps.explanation: The Frobenius norm sums every squared prediction error. Differentiation with respect to B gives twice \(Z^\mathrm{T}\) times the residual.

steps.title: Set the Gradient to Zero
steps.explanation: At the minimum, the normal equation holds, making every feature uncorrelated with the residual.

steps.title: Solve Under Invertibility
steps.explanation: If \(Z^\mathrm{T}Z\) is invertible, left multiplication by its inverse yields the closed-form readout. With collinearity or high dimension, use ridge regularization rather than forcing an inverse.

symbolNotes: N is the number of stimuli, d the number of features, and m the number of neurons. Each column of B contains the readout weights for one neuron.
Estimate B only on the training neural set. If held-out responses influence layer or hyperparameter selection, they no longer constitute an independent test.
derivation.unitsCheck: The units of Z depend on network activations. B has neural-response-units per feature-unit so that ZB and R both use spikes/s or trial counts.
derivation.limitCheck: With only a constant column in Z, the model predicts only each neuron's mean response. If \(d\ge N\) without regularization, training error may be tiny while overfitting is severe.

workedExample.title: A Least-Squares Readout from One Feature
workedExample.problem: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\).
steps: The one-dimensional normal equation gives \(b=(z^\mathrm{T} r)/(z^\mathrm{T} z)\).
For a new stimulus with \(z=4\), prediction is \(4b=100/14\approx 7.14\). Its reliability must be tested against the actual held-out response.
workedExample.result: Training data give \(b\approx 1.786\), and held-out feature 4 maps to \(\mathrm{prediction}\approx 7.14\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: If \(r=2z\) exactly, the formula returns \(b=2\). Here the third point is below 6, so the fitted slope is slightly below 2.

pitfalls: Mistaking the fitting power of a flexible nonlinear mapping for similarity between the original representation and neural representation.
Comparing raw correlations across datasets without accounting for neural-response reliability.

modules.title: E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization
paragraphs: This section places surround effects in an E/I recurrent rate model. One common form is \(\tau _{E} dr_{E}/dt=-r_{E}+F_{E}(w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E})\) and \(\tau _{I} dr_{I}/dt=-r_{I}+F_{I}(w_{\mathrm{IE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{II}} r_{I}+I_{I})\). The weights are positive magnitudes and inhibition already carries a minus sign. Recurrent excitation, feedback inhibition, and external inputs jointly determine the fixed point. One population's firing rate is not identical to the net current it delivers to a target.

Within a piecewise-linear region, temporarily set F to identity. The E-nullcline is \(r_{E}=w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E}\), and the I-nullcline can also be rearranged as a line giving \(r_{I}\) versus \(r_{E}\). Their intersection is the steady state. If surround increases external drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population, it shifts the I-nullcline. In an ISN regime, the added drive initially strengthens inhibition and lowers \(r_{E}\), which then reduces recurrent excitation to I. The new intersection can have lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\).

The ISN has an excitatory subnetwork that would be unstable in isolation—effective recurrent E gain exceeds leak—but fast inhibitory feedback stabilizes the complete E/I network. The name does not mean that inhibitory firing always rises or that every suppression comes from added I input. Under some perturbations, stronger external drive to I lowers its steady-state rate. This paradoxical response arises from network rebalancing and tests ISN structure more directly than simply measuring whether I is large.

Read a nullcline plot in four steps: label both axes and zero-derivative curves; determine where each derivative is positive; locate intersections; and ask whether arrows after a small displacement return to the intersection. An intersection alone does not establish stability. With nonlinear F there may be several intersections, and surround can change gain instead of only shifting input. The linear example exposes causal structure, while realistic fitting must retain nonlinearities and temporal dynamics.
keyPoints: Surround suppression is a shift of the full recurrent fixed point and does not require an increase in inhibitory firing rate.
Nullcline intersections give steady states; local vector fields or Jacobian eigenvalues determine stability.
An ISN has an unstable E-only subsystem but a stable complete E/I loop; it is not merely a network with qualitatively strong inhibition.

derivation.title: Fixed Point, Surround Shift, and Local Stability in a Linear E/I Network
derivation.setup: Within the current operating range, set \(F_{E}\) and \(F_{I}\) to identity, use one positive time constant \(\tau\) for both populations, and choose \(w_{\mathrm{EE}}=1.2\), \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}=1\), \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}=1\), \(w_{\mathrm{II}}=0\). The fixed-point equations are \(0=-r_{E}+1.2r_{E}-r_{I}+I_{E}\) and \(0=-r_{I}+r_{E}+I_{I}\).

steps.title: Express \(r_{I}\) from the I Equation
steps.explanation: The second fixed-point equation directly gives \(r_{I}=r_{E}+I_{I}\); substitute it into the E equation.

steps.title: Solve for \(r_{E}\)
steps.explanation: The E equation becomes \(0.2r_{E}-r_{I}+I_{E}=0\). After substitution and rearrangement, \(0.8r_{E}=I_{E}-I_{I}\).

steps.title: Recover \(r_{I}\) and Compare Conditions
steps.explanation: Compute the new intersection from \(r_{E}\) and then use \(r_{I}=r_{E}+I_{I}\). Both rates can fall when surround input changes.

steps.title: Verify the ISN Conditions with the Jacobian
steps.explanation: The full E/I linearization is \((1/\tau )[[0.2,-1],[1,-1]]\), whose eigenvalues are \((-0.4\pm 0.8i)/\tau\). Their real parts are negative, so the intersection is locally stable. Removing inhibitory feedback leaves E-only eigenvalue \(0.2/\tau >0\), making the isolated E subsystem unstable. These two results—not nullcline intersection by itself—establish that the example is an ISN.

symbolNotes: \(w_{\mathrm{EE}}=1.2\) exceeds unit leak, so the linear E-only subsystem grows. Stability of the full system also depends on inhibitory feedback and time constants.
Identity F applies only locally where rates are positive and unsaturated. A negative calculated rate requires rectification and a new active-set analysis.
derivation.unitsCheck: For rates in spikes/s, dimensionless weights map presynaptic rates into drive of the same units, and \(I_{E}\),\(I_{I}\) are equivalent rate drives. Jacobian eigenvalues contain \(1/\tau\) and therefore have reciprocal-time units.
derivation.limitCheck: Setting \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}\) or \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}\) to zero breaks the stabilizing E/I feedback loop. If E gain exceeds leak, the E-only mode runs away, exposing the ISN condition.

workedExample.title: Surround Suppression with Simultaneous Decreases in E and I Rates
workedExample.problem: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points.
steps: Thus E falls from 10 to 6.25 and I from 12 to 11.25. Although the I population receives more external drive, its steady rate falls slightly because recurrent E input falls more.
workedExample.result: Both steady-state E and I are lower with surround; this does not exclude a role for recurrent inhibition.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Substitution verifies the surround E equation: \(-6.25+1.2\times 6.25-11.25+10=0\); and I equation: \(-11.25+6.25+5=0\).

pitfalls: Conflating inhibitory-population rate, inhibitory current received by a target, and net suppression.
Declaring an intersection stable from the nullclines alone without inspecting the local vector field or Jacobian eigenvalues.

synthesis: Feedforward cascades can construct selectivity and invariance stage by stage, but descriptive blocks do not automatically identify biological mechanisms. Complex cells are approximately invariant to grating phase, so a single linear STA can be zero; a quadrature-pair square-and-sum energy model is a minimal explanation. Surround suppression likewise is not simply “more inhibition”: recurrent E/I dynamics can make excitation and inhibition fall together, with excitation falling more. Nullclines show the fixed-point shift, while Jacobian stability and an unstable E-only subsystem establish an inhibition-stabilized regime.
workedExamples: 【例题】题目：complex cell 对 0° grating 的所有 phases 都响应。
Worked solution. spike-triggered stimuli 含相反 bright/dark phases，linear average 抵消；STC 找到两个 quadrature features，energy output 保持高。 Check. zero first moment 不等于 zero higher-order dependence。
【拓展例题】题目：加 surround 后 excitatory conductance 与 inhibitory conductance 都下降，前者下降更多。
Worked solution. net depolarizing drive 下降，firing suppression 仍可发生；不能以 inhibition 未增加否定 recurrent inhibitory stabilization。 Check. 要比较 net currents/operating point，而不只是单个 conductance direction。
